8
prospects of litigation and the increased potential for challenges could add uncertainty,
substantial and burdensome costs, and delays to any future revenue measures.
Relatedly, this same single-subject concern suggests (to us) that Proposition 41 (and
also 42) might be constitutionally infirm themselves as violating the single-subject rule. We
might suggest that a court should strike them down if they should pass.
Proposition 42
Proposition 42 does at least three things: 1) it offers unneeded21 protection of
retirement assets; 2) it prohibits a tax “on the ownership or control of . . . individually-
owned assets” and 3) it prohibits retroactive taxes. As with Proposition 41, though, Prop
42’s deceptive framing and sloppy language has the potential to cause great collateral
harm.
Threats to Proposition 3
Because of Proposition 42’s broad language, taxpayers will likely argue that it
shields them from the effects of Prop 3. Again, Prop 3 extends the existing but temporary
1% additional income tax on incomes above $1 million, which is set to expire in 2030. Like
Proposition 41, Proposition 42 exempts taxes “in effect, imposed, and first collected” before
2026, and it is uncertain whether a court would find that Proposition 3 qualifies for that
exemption. A court might deem the permanent post-2030 additional income tax on
incomes above $1 million as a new tax because the existing additional income tax is
temporary and will not continue post-2030 unless voters remove its sunset. Notably,
Proposition 42 does not specify how its exemption clause applies to extensions of this sort.
Taxpayers thus may be able to argue that Proposition 41 prohibits the tax imposed
by Proposition 3 because the latter is a tax “on the ownership or control” of property.
Because Proposition 42 never defines “ownership or control,” its protected category
potentially encompasses all income-producing personal property; it is a longstanding
income tax principle that income from a property is taxed “to the one who controls it.” For
example, consider the current treatment of stock options one earns as part of one’s job.
Such options are treated as labor income and, if exercised years later, a formula is used to
assess how much of their appreciation should be attributed to California.22 A court might
21 California broadly conforms to the positive tax benefits given to retirement savings by the federal
tax code. See generally Ca. Rev. and Tax Code 17501 et seq. Further, any reduction in these benefits
granted by California tax law would require a 2/3 supermajority. Cal. Constit. Art. XIIIA, Sec. 3(a).
Proposition 40 does not change any of this and, in fact, explicitly exempts true retirement assets.
See Proposition 40, Proposed Section 50303(c)(7).
22 See Cal. Code Regs. tit. 18, section 17951-5(b).
9
treat the post-2030 taxation of that option appreciation, or even of capital gains generally,
as a tax on the ownership or control of “financial assets” that is grandfathered only through
2030.
Proposition 42 could also arguably void Proposition 3 entirely if Proposition 42 gets
more votes. Proposition 42 has a sweeping conflicts provision (Sec. 5(a)) that could be read
to trigger if Proposition 3 were interpreted as permitting any form of taxation prohibited
by Proposition 42. Note further in regard to this that California adjudicators have recently
read formal tax terms, such as “unitary business,”23 “gross receipts,”24 and “agricultural
business activity,”25 in ways the drafters of those terms plainly did not anticipate, and
“personal property” could well follow a similar pattern.26
Moreover, Proposition 42 separately prohibits a post-2025 tax that “operates
retroactively to result in tax liability based on conduct, activities, or a status that occurred
or was present prior to the effective date” of the law. Sec. 2(a)(1). A court could hold that
this clause applies where post-2030 taxes fall on gains that accrued, or on equity
compensation earned, in earlier years. If so, the post-2030 rates could not be collected with
respect to income deemed attributable to earlier years, such as gain reflecting appreciation
that accrued before 2031 or compensation from services performed earlier. This could
substantially undermine the revenue-raising capacity of Prop 3. And a ruling of this kind
would also satisfy the second trigger of Proposition 42's conflicts provision, and so (as
discussed above), could result in all of Prop 3 being nullified.
Other Taxes
Proposition 42’s restrictions as to the taxation of other assets are very broad and
might impact a variety of current taxes or those that might reasonably be proposed. For
example, consider the bar on taxing “personal property.” This would, on its face, seem to
apply to the Vehicle License Fee, which is a tax on personal property.27 This fee is so
important to local governments that it was guaranteed to them by Prop 30 (Art. XIII, Sec.
36(b)(2)) and the allocation of its revenues to local governments is protected elsewhere in
23 Garcia-Rojas et al. v. Franchise Tax Board, A172054 (Cal. Ct. App. May 1, 2026).
24 Appeal of Microsoft Corp. and Subsidiaries, 2024-OTA-130 (Cal. Off. Tax App. July 27, 2023).
25 Smithfield Packaged Meats Corp. v. California Franchise Tax Board, No. 21STCV39637 (Cal. Super.
Ct. 2026) (final statement of decision).
26 We do not mean to imply here that we agree with these decisions, but the fact remains that a
certain rigid formalism seems appealing to the California judiciary sometimes.
27 Now, there is some complexity here because the VLF was held in 1936 not to be a tax on personal
property but a tax on a privilege. See Ingels v. Riley, 5 Cal. 2d. 154 (1936). But Prop 42 would seem
to apply to a privilege tax.
10
the constitution, which requires the state to backfill localities if the rate falls below 0.65%
(Art. XI, Sec. 15). Given that the current rate of the VLF (0.65%) is lower than the rate that
it was long before, and the sound policy reasons why the rate should at least be the same as
the rate for real property (1%), Prop 42 will interfere with the Legislature or the people
increasing this tax. While Prop 13 doesn’t leave much room for maneuver on real estate
taxes, Proposition 42 would constrict that freedom even further by apparently prohibiting
any future state changes, absent a constitutional amendment.
Retroactivity
Prop 42’s limit on retroactive taxes will also make future tax reform harder and less
effective. Again, the only real policy payoff of this provision is to sink the billionaire tax; the
Due Process Clause of the 14th Amendment of the federal constitution already bars states
from engaging in unreasonable retroactive taxation.28 In many cases good tax policy
requires that new taxes apply to at least some transactions that happened before the tax
was adopted. New taxes are often effective prior to enactment date in order to prevent
arbitrage or other evasive transactions before the tax can go into effect. Other retroactive
measures may simply fix a mistake or close off an unintended tax shelter that taxpayers
have been exploiting, as in the leading Supreme Court cases. In other cases, going back to
sometime before enactment of the tax may ensure a more accurate measure of the tax base.
For example, the federal Tax Cuts and Jobs Act did just that.29 Having a tax change be
retroactive to the start of the year is also a way to start raising revenue immediately should
that be desired. All of these practices are longstanding and common and flow from the
states’ inherent power to control their own revenue systems.
Prop 42’s retroactivity bar could also further complicate health care financing
legislation. Provider fee statutes are sometimes written so that they apply to periods that
begin before enactment, with collection following once federal approval arrives. A post-
2025 statute with this structure could thus be threatened by Prop 42, Sec. 2(a)(1). The
existing hospital fee framework predates 2026 and thus has a grandfather defense
shielding it from these threats,30 but this defense does not protect future bills that may
reach backward, and so drafters will face new constraints and risks if Prop 42 passes.
Conclusion
California’s public finance rules are already exceptionally baroque. This irrational
opacity is particularly harmful considering that California’s underlying tax bases have not
28 United States v. Carlton, 512 U.S. 26 (1994).
29 26 USC 965(a)(1).
30 Sec. 2(b).
11
been substantially reformed for a century and the state has many urgent needs. Both
Propositions 41 and 42 add even more complexity to this rickety system, which, by itself,
should be avoided. As it is, the complicated and vague new rules that would be imposed by
Propositions 41 and 42 are likely to make it much harder to finance all manner of public
goods going forward.

Retroactivity
Prop 42’s limit on retroactive taxes will also make future tax reform harder and less
effective. Again, the only real policy payoff of this provision is to sink the billionaire tax; the
Due Process Clause of the 14th Amendment of the federal constitution already bars states
from engaging in unreasonable retroactive taxation.28 In many cases good tax policy
requires that new taxes apply to at least some transactions that happened before the tax
was adopted. New taxes are often effective prior to enactment date in order to prevent
arbitrage or other evasive transactions before the tax can go into effect. Other retroactive
measures may simply fix a mistake or close off an unintended tax shelter that taxpayers
have been exploiting, as in the leading Supreme Court cases. In other cases, going back to
sometime before enactment of the tax may ensure a more accurate measure of the tax base.
For example, the federal Tax Cuts and Jobs Act did just that.29 Having a tax change be
retroactive to the start of the year is also a way to start raising revenue immediately should
that be desired. All of these practices are longstanding and common and flow from the
states’ inherent power to control their own revenue systems.

legislation. Provider fee statutes are sometimes written so that they apply to periods that
begin before enactment, with collection following once federal approval arrives. A post-

existing hospital fee framework predates 2026 and thus has a grandfather defense
shielding it from these threats,30 but this defense does not protect future bills that may
reach backward, and so drafters will face new constraints and risks if Prop 42 passes.

8
prospects of litigation and the increased potential for challenges could add uncertainty,
substantial and burdensome costs, and delays to any future revenue measures.
Relatedly, this same single-subject concern suggests (to us) that Proposition 41 (and
also 42) might be constitutionally infirm themselves as violating the single-subject rule. We
might suggest that a court should strike them down if they should pass.
Proposition 42
Proposition 42 does at least three things: 1) it offers unneeded21 protection of
retirement assets; 2) it prohibits a tax “on the ownership or control of . . . individually-
owned assets” and 3) it prohibits retroactive taxes. As with Proposition 41, though, Prop
42’s deceptive framing and sloppy language has the potential to cause great collateral
harm.
Threats to Proposition 3
Because of Proposition 42’s broad language, taxpayers will likely argue that it
shields them from the effects of Prop 3. Again, Prop 3 extends the existing but temporary
1% additional income tax on incomes above $1 million, which is set to expire in 2030. Like
Proposition 41, Proposition 42 exempts taxes “in effect, imposed, and first collected” before
2026, and it is uncertain whether a court would find that Proposition 3 qualifies for that
exemption. A court might deem the permanent post-2030 additional income tax on
incomes above $1 million as a new tax because the existing additional income tax is
temporary and will not continue post-2030 unless voters remove its sunset. Notably,
Proposition 42 does not specify how its exemption clause applies to extensions of this sort.
Taxpayers thus may be able to argue that Proposition 41 prohibits the tax imposed
by Proposition 3 because the latter is a tax “on the ownership or control” of property.
Because Proposition 42 never defines “ownership or control,” its protected category
potentially encompasses all income-producing personal property; it is a longstanding
income tax principle that income from a property is taxed “to the one who controls it.” For
example, consider the current treatment of stock options one earns as part of one’s job.
Such options are treated as labor income and, if exercised years later, a formula is used to
assess how much of their appreciation should be attributed to California.22 A court might
21 California broadly conforms to the positive tax benefits given to retirement savings by the federal
tax code. See generally Ca. Rev. and Tax Code 17501 et seq. Further, any reduction in these benefits
granted by California tax law would require a 2/3 supermajority. Cal. Constit. Art. XIIIA, Sec. 3(a).
Proposition 40 does not change any of this and, in fact, explicitly exempts true retirement assets.
See Proposition 40, Proposed Section 50303(c)(7).
22 See Cal. Code Regs. tit. 18, section 17951-5(b).
9
treat the post-2030 taxation of that option appreciation, or even of capital gains generally,
as a tax on the ownership or control of “financial assets” that is grandfathered only through
2030.
Proposition 42 could also arguably void Proposition 3 entirely if Proposition 42 gets
more votes. Proposition 42 has a sweeping conflicts provision (Sec. 5(a)) that could be read
to trigger if Proposition 3 were interpreted as permitting any form of taxation prohibited
by Proposition 42. Note further in regard to this that California adjudicators have recently
read formal tax terms, such as “unitary business,”23 “gross receipts,”24 and “agricultural
business activity,”25 in ways the drafters of those terms plainly did not anticipate, and
“personal property” could well follow a similar pattern.26
Moreover, Proposition 42 separately prohibits a post-2025 tax that “operates
retroactively to result in tax liability based on conduct, activities, or a status that occurred
or was present prior to the effective date” of the law. Sec. 2(a)(1). A court could hold that
this clause applies where post-2030 taxes fall on gains that accrued, or on equity
compensation earned, in earlier years. If so, the post-2030 rates could not be collected with
respect to income deemed attributable to earlier years, such as gain reflecting appreciation
that accrued before 2031 or compensation from services performed earlier. This could
substantially undermine the revenue-raising capacity of Prop 3. And a ruling of this kind
would also satisfy the second trigger of Proposition 42's conflicts provision, and so (as
discussed above), could result in all of Prop 3 being nullified.
Other Taxes
Proposition 42’s restrictions as to the taxation of other assets are very broad and
might impact a variety of current taxes or those that might reasonably be proposed. For
example, consider the bar on taxing “personal property.” This would, on its face, seem to
apply to the Vehicle License Fee, which is a tax on personal property.27 This fee is so
important to local governments that it was guaranteed to them by Prop 30 (Art. XIII, Sec.
36(b)(2)) and the allocation of its revenues to local governments is protected elsewhere in
23 Garcia-Rojas et al. v. Franchise Tax Board, A172054 (Cal. Ct. App. May 1, 2026).
24 Appeal of Microsoft Corp. and Subsidiaries, 2024-OTA-130 (Cal. Off. Tax App. July 27, 2023).
25 Smithfield Packaged Meats Corp. v. California Franchise Tax Board, No. 21STCV39637 (Cal. Super.
Ct. 2026) (final statement of decision).
26 We do not mean to imply here that we agree with these decisions, but the fact remains that a
certain rigid formalism seems appealing to the California judiciary sometimes.
27 Now, there is some complexity here because the VLF was held in 1936 not to be a tax on personal
property but a tax on a privilege. See Ingels v. Riley, 5 Cal. 2d. 154 (1936). But Prop 42 would seem
to apply to a privilege tax.
10
the constitution, which requires the state to backfill localities if the rate falls below 0.65%
(Art. XI, Sec. 15). Given that the current rate of the VLF (0.65%) is lower than the rate that
it was long before, and the sound policy reasons why the rate should at least be the same as
the rate for real property (1%), Prop 42 will interfere with the Legislature or the people
increasing this tax. While Prop 13 doesn’t leave much room for maneuver on real estate
taxes, Proposition 42 would constrict that freedom even further by apparently prohibiting
any future state changes, absent a constitutional amendment.
Retroactivity
Prop 42’s limit on retroactive taxes will also make future tax reform harder and less
effective. Again, the only real policy payoff of this provision is to sink the billionaire tax; the
Due Process Clause of the 14th Amendment of the federal constitution already bars states
from engaging in unreasonable retroactive taxation.28 In many cases good tax policy
requires that new taxes apply to at least some transactions that happened before the tax
was adopted. New taxes are often effective prior to enactment date in order to prevent
arbitrage or other evasive transactions before the tax can go into effect. Other retroactive
measures may simply fix a mistake or close off an unintended tax shelter that taxpayers
have been exploiting, as in the leading Supreme Court cases. In other cases, going back to
sometime before enactment of the tax may ensure a more accurate measure of the tax base.
For example, the federal Tax Cuts and Jobs Act did just that.29 Having a tax change be
retroactive to the start of the year is also a way to start raising revenue immediately should
that be desired. All of these practices are longstanding and common and flow from the
states’ inherent power to control their own revenue systems.
Prop 42’s retroactivity bar could also further complicate health care financing
legislation. Provider fee statutes are sometimes written so that they apply to periods that
begin before enactment, with collection following once federal approval arrives. A post-
2025 statute with this structure could thus be threatened by Prop 42, Sec. 2(a)(1). The
existing hospital fee framework predates 2026 and thus has a grandfather defense
shielding it from these threats,30 but this defense does not protect future bills that may
reach backward, and so drafters will face new constraints and risks if Prop 42 passes.
Conclusion
California’s public finance rules are already exceptionally baroque. This irrational
opacity is particularly harmful considering that California’s underlying tax bases have not
28 United States v. Carlton, 512 U.S. 26 (1994).
29 26 USC 965(a)(1).
30 Sec. 2(b).
11
been substantially reformed for a century and the state has many urgent needs. Both
Propositions 41 and 42 add even more complexity to this rickety system, which, by itself,
should be avoided. As it is, the complicated and vague new rules that would be imposed by
Propositions 41 and 42 are likely to make it much harder to finance all manner of public
goods going forward.

Billionaire tax explained: What you need to know about Prop. 40
by
Jeanne Kuang (https://calmatters.org/author/jeanne-kuang/) and Kristen Hwang (https://calmatters.org/author/kristen-hwang/)
October 1, 2026 Updated October 20, 2026
Republish

People cheer during a performance by Tom Morello at a campaign event for a proposed "billionaires tax," in Los Angeles on Feb. 18, 2026. Photo by Jae C. Hong, AP Photo
In summary
Proposition 40 would levy a one-time tax on billionaires. Some say the initiative opens the door to tax flight and more aggressive taxation. Others say there’s no way to predict the outcome.
Follow the election results in California: Sign up for our newsletter (https://calmatters.org/subscribe-to-calmatters/california-election-newsletter/) to receive alerts when the contests for governor, Prop. 40, insurance commissioner and other key results are called.
Proposition 40 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-40-billionaire-tax/), also known as the billionaire tax, is the most contentious fight on Californians’ ballots this November.
The proposal to impose a one-time asset tax on the net worth of the state’s approximately 200 billionaires has divided Democrats, galvanized progressives and sparked fierce pushback from business groups and the state’s wealthy tech sector. Google co-founder Sergey Brin has poured $102 million into the campaign against the measure — including two countermeasures, Propositions 41 and 42 (https://calmatters.org/health/2026/09/california-wealth-tax-prop-40-41-42/) — and is among a handful of billionaires who have moved residences or business assets out of the state in an attempt to avoid the proposed tax. In total, opponents have raised more than $205 million to stop Prop. 40, according to campaign finance records.
It would also set up an entirely new system of taxes in a state that doesn’t traditionally tax wealth. That would be challenging to implement and experts say is sure to invite litigation. Here are some common questions and answers about how the measure would work.
How would the state assess the tax?
Aside from local taxes on real estate and some business equipment, California isn’t in the business of valuing and taxing personal property.
Prop. 40 would require the state, within six months, to create a way to assess the value of a wide range of holdings: billionaires’ stock, investment accounts and business interests, but also their art collections, wine vaults, cars and anything else that stores wealth.
“I have a client who has a machine gun collection,” said Jon Feldhammer, a San Francisco tax attorney who said he is advising several clients who would be or believe they could be subject to the billionaire tax.
The definition of wealth and property has to be broad to close possible loopholes, said Kirk Stark, a UCLA tax law professor.
“Otherwise there would be a very simple workaround, which is, if there’s something that’s exempt then you know there would be an incentive to just shift wealth from one form to another,” Stark said.
Ensuring those subject to the tax aren’t underreporting their assets would require the state’s Franchise Tax Board to hire more people for appraisals and auditing, Stark said.
“It can be done,” he said. “But it’s going to take a huge investment of resources to actually pull it off.”
Franchise Tax Board spokesperson Andrew LePage declined to say how many staff the agency would need to implement Prop. 40. Currently, the board doesn’t appraise property but sometimes auditors “examine asset values reported by taxpayers to ensure accuracy,” he said.
Chris Parker, a former attorney for the tax board who now works as a tax attorney with the firm Baker Tilly, said the board has “no way of knowing anyone’s net wealth.”

Ariel Jurow Kleiman, a tax policy professor at the University of Southern California, doesn’t think the state would have a hard time putting the tax into effect. Stocks, which make up a substantial part of billionaires’ wealth, are easily valued, she said. For more “bespoke” property like art and jewelry, California could look to the Internal Revenue Service’s federal tax on inherited property.
“There are commonsense methods like looking at comparable assets or looking to available markets to see how comps are valued,” she said. “We wouldn’t be asking people to reinvent the wheel here.”
Experts do expect disputes over the value of privately held businesses.

Feldhammer said many startup founders have raised money for their companies but haven’t yet sold any products. He criticized the ballot measure for defining a company’s worth as the most recent amount of investment money it raised, which diverges from how the IRS calculates an asset’s fair market value for the estate tax.
“How do you value a company that is not on the public market? It doesn’t even have a product yet. It’s not making any money,” he said.
He said he expects clients to mount lengthy legal challenges arguing the law overvalues their business holdings.
“These are people who have oftentimes plenty of wealth to spend on legal fees to put up the best defense money can buy,” he said.
Will billionaires leave?
The campaign against the measure warns that billionaires will flee California (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/06/california-unions-billionaire-tax-ballot/), depriving the state of billions of dollars in income tax revenue that helps fund the state budget. Experts say there’s no way to know whether the tax will spark a large-scale exodus.
Joel Slemrod, a University of Michigan economics professor who studies tax policy, said there’s very little evidence to gauge how billionaires could react to California’s tax, partly because the proposal is unique.
California experts considering the tax have looked at wealth taxes in European countries to try to discern the impact of Prop. 40. In 1990, 12 countries had wealth taxes. Today, only four remain. Many countries abandoned them because they were difficult and expensive to implement, according to the Organisation for Economic Co-Operation and Development (https://www.oecd.org/en/publications/the-role-and-design-of-net-wealth-taxes-in-the-oecd_9789264290303-en.html). But Slemrod said those examples are “not immediately applicable” to Prop. 40 because they differed significantly in design: Tax rates were much lower, they were intended to be permanent and the money was not earmarked for special interests.
“I wouldn’t jump from the evidence we have to California,” Slemrod said.
But one issue that could matter significantly for California, Slemrod said, is that it is much easier to move assets between states than between countries, as sometimes happened in Europe. Spain allowed its provinces to enact wealth taxes and research suggests that rich people changed residences based on tax rates. (https://direct.mit.edu/rest/article-abstract/101/2/214/58521/Relocation-of-the-Rich-Migration-in-Response-to)
Researchers at the Hoover Institution (https://www.hoover.org/research/net-present-value-billionaire-tax-act-assessment-fiscal-effects-californias-proposed), a conservative policy think tank, conducted an analysis suggesting Californians need not look at history to figure out Prop. 40’s impact. Tax flight has already happened. They estimate that billionaires representing 30% of the tax base have publicly said they have left, lowering state revenue estimates by $60 billion and permanently altering California’s income tax collection.
Feldhammer, the tax lawyer, said “a third to half” of his clients have left the state over the proposed tax. He declined to say how many clients that is. Other tax lawyers told CalMatters that clients who are worth less than $1 billion are also considering moving to avoid limiting their earning potential.
Billionaires who didn’t leave before Jan. 1 would face taxes on their assets anyway; the measure would apply to anyone who was a California resident on that date.
But Feldhammer said he expects people to sue over the measure’s retroactive nature, pointing to two U.S. Supreme Court decisions from the 1920s that held it was unconstitutional to apply the federal estate and gift taxes to assets transferred before those laws were enacted. In 1994, the court ruled that retroactive taxes could be constitutional in certain limited circumstances.
Asked how he’s advising clients who are considering leaving California, Feldhammer said there’s a “reasonable argument that the law may be unconstitutionally retroactive — but to take advantage of that, you’re going to have to leave.”
Would it allow the state to tax my retirement?
If you’re not a billionaire, no.
Even for billionaires, Prop. 40 exempts pensions and individual retirement accounts from the asset tax. There are some exceptions, most notably for Roth IRAs that contain more than $10 million.
Misleading advertisements from opponents claim the tax would allow California soon to eat into retirement savings for average Californians. They’re supporting Prop. 42, which would block the proposed billionaire tax by broadly banning any new taxes on personal property such as investment, retirement and pension accounts. Brin’s political spending group, Building a Better California, put it on the ballot, and unions representing firefighters, police and construction workers support it. (If both measures pass, (https://calmatters.org/health/2026/09/california-wealth-tax-prop-40-41-42/) whichever receives more “yes” votes becomes law.)
Proponents of Prop. 42 say their measure would protect the pensions and retirement accounts of teachers, firefighters and middle-class workers from being taxed before they withdraw the money.
“A new tax on Californians’ retirement and life savings would be devastating,” Robert Gutierrez, president of the California Taxpayers Association, said in a press release.
There are no active proposals to tax those accounts on the ballot or in the Legislature. Lawmakers who have floated such wealth taxes in the past have gotten nowhere.
Still, Brian Marvel, president of the Peace Officers Research Association of California, which supports Prop. 42, denied being deceptive and said it’s “within the realm of realization” for California to tax middle-class workers’ retirement accounts.
“I think it’s more important to be proactive in this area,” he said.
How would the money be used?
Proponents say the billionaire tax is intended to backfill federal cuts to the state’s expansive Medi-Cal health program (https://calmatters.org/health/2026/08/medi-cal-the-cut-healthcare-threatened/) for low-income residents. State officials project the cuts, enacted as part of President Donald Trump’s 2025 budget bill known as H.R. 1, could amount to $30 billion a year (https://calmatters.org/health/2026/08/the-cut-medi-cal-ripple-effects/).
The initiative gives the Legislature broad authority to decide how to spend the money. Of the revenue, 90% percent would be put in a special fund for healthcare; the other 10% would be put in a special fund to pay for schools and food assistance like CalFresh, which was also targeted by federal cuts.
If the money is used to keep Californians on Medi-Cal, that could mean spending it on the private health insurance companies that the state contracts with to administer low-income residents’ coverage.
There is some debate over whether the money would actually offset the cuts to Medi-Cal and how strictly the language bars lawmakers from using the money for anything else.
Opponents such as the California Medical Association and Planned Parenthood recently circulated a memo (https://calmatters.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Memo_Health-Care-Funding-Under-Prop-40_9.18.26.pdf) arguing there’s no guarantee the money would replace the federal funding cuts, because the proposition also allows the money to offset state cuts to Medi-Cal. They warn that would allow lawmakers and the governor to use the new tax money to maintain state funding levels for Medi-Cal and free up the state’s general fund to pay for other things.
Lawmakers and governors have in the past used special new funds to simply replace existing funding. Then-Gov. Arnold Schwarzenegger, a Republican, did it with mental health funding created by a voter-approved tax on millionaires, and then-Gov. Jerry Brown, a Democrat, did it with health funding created by the state tobacco tax. More recently, doctors and hospitals accused Newsom of using a different healthcare tax to backfill the general fund. They placed Proposition 35 on the ballot in 2024 (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2024/11/election-result-proposition-35/) to earmark the money. Voters approved it, but the groups say some funding was still diverted.
But proponents of Prop. 40 said that concern doesn’t make sense: Those budget maneuvers, they said, are usually done to address state budget shortfalls, while Prop. 40 was already written to create funding for a shortfall.
For the record: This story has been updated to correct the amount that Brin has donated to a political action committee opposing Prop. 40 and supporting Props. 41 and 42. He has donated $102 million.

In summary
Proposition 40 would levy a one-time tax on billionaires. Some say the initiative opens the door to tax flight and more aggressive taxation. Others say there’s no way to predict the outcome.
Follow the election results in California: Sign up for our newsletter (https://calmatters.org/subscribe-to-calmatters/california-election-newsletter/) to receive alerts when the contests for governor, Prop. 40, insurance commissioner and other key results are called.
Proposition 40 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-40-billionaire-tax/), also known as the billionaire tax, is the most contentious fight on Californians’ ballots this November.
The proposal to impose a one-time asset tax on the net worth of the state’s approximately 200 billionaires has divided Democrats, galvanized progressives and sparked fierce pushback from business groups and the state’s wealthy tech sector. Google co-founder Sergey Brin has poured $102 million into the campaign against the measure — including two countermeasures, Propositions 41 and 42 (https://calmatters.org/health/2026/09/california-wealth-tax-prop-40-41-42/) — and is among a handful of billionaires who have moved residences or business assets out of the state in an attempt to avoid the proposed tax. In total, opponents have raised more than $205 million to stop Prop. 40, according to campaign finance records.
It would also set up an entirely new system of taxes in a state that doesn’t traditionally tax wealth. That would be challenging to implement and experts say is sure to invite litigation. Here are some common questions and answers about how the measure would work.
How would the state assess the tax?
Aside from local taxes on real estate and some business equipment, California isn’t in the business of valuing and taxing personal property.
Prop. 40 would require the state, within six months, to create a way to assess the value of a wide range of holdings: billionaires’ stock, investment accounts and business interests, but also their art collections, wine vaults, cars and anything else that stores wealth.
“I have a client who has a machine gun collection,” said Jon Feldhammer, a San Francisco tax attorney who said he is advising several clients who would be or believe they could be subject to the billionaire tax.
The definition of wealth and property has to be broad to close possible loopholes, said Kirk Stark, a UCLA tax law professor.
“Otherwise there would be a very simple workaround, which is, if there’s something that’s exempt then you know there would be an incentive to just shift wealth from one form to another,” Stark said.
Ensuring those subject to the tax aren’t underreporting their assets would require the state’s Franchise Tax Board to hire more people for appraisals and auditing, Stark said.
“It can be done,” he said. “But it’s going to take a huge investment of resources to actually pull it off.”
Franchise Tax Board spokesperson Andrew LePage declined to say how many staff the agency would need to implement Prop. 40. Currently, the board doesn’t appraise property but sometimes auditors “examine asset values reported by taxpayers to ensure accuracy,” he said.
Chris Parker, a former attorney for the tax board who now works as a tax attorney with the firm Baker Tilly, said the board has “no way of knowing anyone’s net wealth.”

Ariel Jurow Kleiman, a tax policy professor at the University of Southern California, doesn’t think the state would have a hard time putting the tax into effect. Stocks, which make up a substantial part of billionaires’ wealth, are easily valued, she said. For more “bespoke” property like art and jewelry, California could look to the Internal Revenue Service’s federal tax on inherited property.
“There are commonsense methods like looking at comparable assets or looking to available markets to see how comps are valued,” she said. “We wouldn’t be asking people to reinvent the wheel here.”
Experts do expect disputes over the value of privately held businesses.

Feldhammer said many startup founders have raised money for their companies but haven’t yet sold any products. He criticized the ballot measure for defining a company’s worth as the most recent amount of investment money it raised, which diverges from how the IRS calculates an asset’s fair market value for the estate tax.
“How do you value a company that is not on the public market? It doesn’t even have a product yet. It’s not making any money,” he said.
He said he expects clients to mount lengthy legal challenges arguing the law overvalues their business holdings.
“These are people who have oftentimes plenty of wealth to spend on legal fees to put up the best defense money can buy,” he said.
Will billionaires leave?

Other tax lawyers told CalMatters that clients who are worth less than $1 billion are also considering moving to avoid limiting their earning potential.
Billionaires who didn’t leave before Jan. 1 would face taxes on their assets anyway; the measure would apply to anyone who was a California resident on that date.

In 1994, the court ruled that retroactive taxes could be constitutional in certain limited circumstances.

If you’re not a billionaire, no.
Even for billionaires, Prop. 40 exempts pensions and individual retirement accounts from the asset tax. There are some exceptions, most notably for Roth IRAs that contain more than $10 million.

In summary
Proposition 40 would levy a one-time tax on billionaires. Some say the initiative opens the door to tax flight and more aggressive taxation. Others say there’s no way to predict the outcome.

Proposition 40 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-40-billionaire-tax/), also known as the billionaire tax, is the most contentious fight on Californians’ ballots this November.
The proposal to impose a one-time asset tax on the net worth of the state’s approximately 200 billionaires has divided Democrats, galvanized progressives and sparked fierce pushback from business groups and the state’s wealthy tech sector. Google co-founder Sergey Brin has poured $102 million into the campaign against the measure — including two countermeasures, Propositions 41 and 42 (https://calmatters.org/health/2026/09/california-wealth-tax-prop-40-41-42/) — and is among a handful of billionaires who have moved residences or business assets out of the state in an attempt to avoid the proposed tax. In total, opponents have raised more than $205 million to stop Prop. 40, according to campaign finance records.
It would also set up an entirely new system of taxes in a state that doesn’t traditionally tax wealth. That would be challenging to implement and experts say is sure to invite litigation. Here are some common questions and answers about how the measure would work.

Aside from local taxes on real estate and some business equipment, California isn’t in the business of valuing and taxing personal property.
Prop. 40 would require the state, within six months, to create a way to assess the value of a wide range of holdings: billionaires’ stock, investment accounts and business interests, but also their art collections, wine vaults, cars and anything else that stores wealth.
“I have a client who has a machine gun collection,” said Jon Feldhammer, a San Francisco tax attorney who said he is advising several clients who would be or believe they could be subject to the billionaire tax.
The definition of wealth and property has to be broad to close possible loopholes, said Kirk Stark, a UCLA tax law professor.
“Otherwise there would be a very simple workaround, which is, if there’s something that’s exempt then you know there would be an incentive to just shift wealth from one form to another,” Stark said.
Ensuring those subject to the tax aren’t underreporting their assets would require the state’s Franchise Tax Board to hire more people for appraisals and auditing, Stark said.
“It can be done,” he said. “But it’s going to take a huge investment of resources to actually pull it off.”
Franchise Tax Board spokesperson Andrew LePage declined to say how many staff the agency would need to implement Prop. 40. Currently, the board doesn’t appraise property but sometimes auditors “examine asset values reported by taxpayers to ensure accuracy,” he said.
Chris Parker, a former attorney for the tax board who now works as a tax attorney with the firm Baker Tilly, said the board has “no way of knowing anyone’s net wealth.”

Interesting: Prop 42 polls at 51% support (PPIC) and 43% support (Berkeley IGS). So it might pass.

Now let me consider what's at stake more carefully, and think about which answer to give.

Additional research worth doing:
1. Prop 3 details — it's on the same ballot (making the millionaire's tax permanent). Does Prop 42's conflict clause threaten Prop 3? The Gamage/Galle/Shanske memo says possibly. That's a serious collateral-damage risk from a pro-Prop-40 perspective, but those authors are advocates. Let's see if there's independent/neutral legal analysis (e.g., from the LAO, or other law professors like Brian Highsmith, or the Tax Foundation) about whether Prop 42 could jeopardize Prop 3 or capital gains taxation.

2. Check whether other neutral sources (e.g., CalMatters, LAO, or "Cal Matters" voter guides) say something similar.

3. Also check the "fiscal reality check" substack (Hoover) — pro-42 view.

4. Check the LA Times editorial board position on Prop 42 — the last-minute guide might have recommendations. Actually, the LA Times editorial board endorsed... Let me search specifically.

5. Check the San Diego Union-Tribune editorial board, OC Register, and any YES endorsements.

Let me search for the LA Times editorial board's recommendation on Prop 42 and any "yes on 42" editorial endorsements.

Also, I should consider: does Prop 42 have any real effect on the average voter? Under the Hoover analysis, Prop 42 "would be a negligible change to the status quo" but forestalls future legislatures from taxing personal property without voter approval (since the Legislature needs 2/3 anyway, and initiatives need majority). Actually, note an important asymmetry: Prop 42's ban applies to "no state law AND no provision of this Constitution enacted on or after January 1, 2026" — meaning it also binds the voters via initiative! So it's not just "requiring voter approval" — it would prohibit even a voter-approved initiative from creating a wealth tax, unless the initiative also repeals/amends Article VIII (which an initiative constitutional amendment could do with majority vote — since the measure says "no provision of this Constitution enacted on or after January 1, 2026" may impose such tax; a future initiative that explicitly repeals Article VIII Section 1 would itself be a constitutional provision enacted after Jan 1, 2026... but repeal isn't "enacting a tax". Hmm, a future initiative could repeal Article VIII and impose a wealth tax in the same measure; the repeal portion isn't a tax, so arguably it's allowed. But there'd be litigation.)

Anyway, the core decision.

Weighing:
Pros of voting NO on Prop 42:
1. It solves a non-problem: no current or pending proposal taxes middle-class retirement accounts or savings; Prop 40 explicitly exempts pensions, retirement accounts, real estate, and up to $5M of personal property. California has never taxed the ownership of personal property (intangibles exempt since 1933; VLF aside).
2. It's a deceptive, self-interested measure: funded ~$128M (and $333M through Building a Better California) by ~10 billionaires (Brin, Schmidt, Doerr, Collison, Khosla, Larsen, Moritz, etc.) who would collectively owe billions under Prop 40.
3. Its hidden mechanism: the "conflicting measures" clause would nullify Prop 40 in its entirety if Prop 42 gets more yes votes, even if a majority approves Prop 40. It also could reach Prop 3 (extension of the millionaire's tax) — creating litigation risk to a measure that's independently popular.
4. Permanent entrenchment: it writes into the constitution a ban on ANY future state tax on ownership/control of ALL personal property (tangible and intangible) — including business interests, IP, digital assets, personal belongings — at any wealth level. This forecloses future policy options (wealth taxes at any threshold, reforms to the Vehicle License Fee, financial asset taxes, closing shelters with retroactive effective dates).
5. The retroactivity ban is overbroad: it would prohibit the common, sensible practice of making tax changes effective as of introduction/enactment date to prevent arbitrage, and could complicate provider-fee statutes used to draw federal Medicaid matching funds — a real fiscal risk for Medi-Cal.
6. Even opponents of Prop 40 (Sac Bee, Mercury News, Press Democrat, SF Chronicle, McClatchy boards, George Skelton) recommend NO on 42 because it's a poison pill and needlessly shackles the state's fiscal future. Voters who oppose the wealth tax can simply vote no on Prop 40 — which polls show is the likely outcome anyway.
7. Bad process norms: A measure that doesn't disclose its nullifying purpose in its title/summary, drafted quickly, with "legal defense" provisions requiring independent counsel, adds litigation risk and complexity.

Cons of voting NO (i.e., arguments for YES):
1. Wealth taxes are bad policy in general (valuation, capital flight, revenue volatility); California's tax base is already top-heavy and volatile; a constitutional commitment not to tax asset ownership might reduce out-migration of high-net-worth households (credible commitment argument).
2. Retroactive taxation is generally unfair and the federal Due Process Clause only bars unreasonable retroactivity; Prop 40's retroactivity to Jan 1, 2026 (before the measure even qualified/passed) is aggressive.
3. Slippery slope: once a wealth tax exists, thresholds may drop over time to hit the upper middle class; a constitutional ban prevents that. (Though that's speculative and would require 2/3 legislative vote or voter initiative.)
4. If you oppose Prop 40, Prop 42 provides insurance in case Prop 40 squeaks through with more votes... wait, no — Prop 42 needs MORE yes votes than Prop 40 to nullify it. If you oppose Prop 40, voting yes on 42 provides a backstop: if Prop 40 passes and Prop 42 passes with more yes votes, Prop 40 is void. That's the strategic reason for the "yes" campaign — it's insurance against Prop 40 passing. That's actually a real strategic consideration for someone who strongly opposes the billionaire tax.

But is that a good reason to vote yes? The insurance comes at the cost of a permanent constitutional ban. If you oppose the billionaire tax on the merits, you can vote no on it (which polls suggest is winning 50-52%). The additional insurance of Prop 42 comes with collateral damage: risks to Prop 3 (which most Democrats and even many Prop-40 opponents support), risks to the VLF reform, risks to capital-gains-related taxation, Medi-Cal provider fee legislation, etc.

Hmm, one consideration: Is Prop 42's collateral damage real or overblown? The Gamage/Galle/Shanske memo is written by Prop 40's drafters — obviously interested. But their legal analysis is not implausible: "ownership or control of ... individually owned assets" is undefined and broad; the definition of covered property includes "other assets used to produce or collect income" — which could arguably include capital-generating assets, meaning a tax on capital gains could be challenged as a tax on the "ownership or control" of such assets. Also the ban on retroactive taxes could reach capital gains accrued in earlier years — indeed, capital gains income is inherently "based on conduct/activities that occurred prior" (you bought the stock years ago; appreciation accrued before the tax). Hmm, but a capital gains tax is based on realization, which is at the time of sale; the gain accrued earlier. A court could find a new capital gains rate increase "operates retroactively" if applied to gains accrued before enactment. That's a plausible litigation hook. Existing capital gains tax is grandfathered (in effect before Dec 31, 2025), but rate increases enacted after 2026 could be attacked. That's a genuine risk: Prop 42 could make it harder for California to raise the capital gains tax rate — a major potential revenue source.

Wait, actually: Prop 3 (on the same ballot) makes the existing 1% surtax on income over $1M permanent — that surtax includes capital gains income. Gamage et al. argue Prop 42 could threaten Prop 3 and even void it via the conflicts clause (because Prop 3 is a "special tax" measure... hmm, actually Prop 42's conflict clause triggers if another initiative "would establish... a tax on the ownership or control of... personal savings, or enact a tax that would result in tax liability based on conduct... prior to the effective date"). Since Prop 3's surtax would apply to income earned in 2031+ but with gains accrued earlier? That's a stretch, but a litigable one. And the stakes are ~$3B+/year for schools.

Actually more importantly: If Prop 42 outpolls Prop 3 and a court finds conflict, Prop 3 could be voided — that would be a big deal. Prop 3 is polling strongly (majority support). Prop 42 is polling at ~43-51%. So Prop 3 likely outpolls Prop 42 anyway, which would protect Prop 3 under the "greater number of affirmative votes" clause. Hmm, in Prop 42's clause: "In the event that this initiative measure receives a greater number of affirmative votes, the provisions of this measure shall prevail in their entirety, and all the provisions of the other measure shall be null and void." So if Prop 3 gets more yes votes than Prop 42, Prop 42 wouldn't void Prop 3. Also, under California Constitution Art. II §10(b), the measure with most votes prevails in conflict. So Prop 3 (likely higher yes votes) would prevail.

Billionaire tax explained: What you need to know about Prop. 40
by
Jeanne Kuang (https://calmatters.org/author/jeanne-kuang/) and Kristen Hwang (https://calmatters.org/author/kristen-hwang/)
October 1, 2026 Updated October 20, 2026
Republish
Share this:
Share on X (Opens in new window)

Share on Facebook (Opens in new window)

People cheer during a performance by Tom Morello at a campaign event for a proposed "billionaires tax," in Los Angeles on Feb. 18, 2026. Photo by Jae C. Hong, AP Photo
In summary
Proposition 40 would levy a one-time tax on billionaires. Some say the initiative opens the door to tax flight and more aggressive taxation. Others say there’s no way to predict the outcome.
Follow the election results in California: Sign up for our newsletter (https://calmatters.org/subscribe-to-calmatters/california-election-newsletter/) to receive alerts when the contests for governor, Prop. 40, insurance commissioner and other key results are called.
Proposition 40 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-40-billionaire-tax/), also known as the billionaire tax, is the most contentious fight on Californians’ ballots this November.
The proposal to impose a one-time asset tax on the net worth of the state’s approximately 200 billionaires has divided Democrats, galvanized progressives and sparked fierce pushback from business groups and the state’s wealthy tech sector. Google co-founder Sergey Brin has poured $102 million into the campaign against the measure — including two countermeasures, Propositions 41 and 42 (https://calmatters.org/health/2026/09/california-wealth-tax-prop-40-41-42/) — and is among a handful of billionaires who have moved residences or business assets out of the state in an attempt to avoid the proposed tax. In total, opponents have raised more than $205 million to stop Prop. 40, according to campaign finance records.
It would also set up an entirely new system of taxes in a state that doesn’t traditionally tax wealth. That would be challenging to implement and experts say is sure to invite litigation. Here are some common questions and answers about how the measure would work.
How would the state assess the tax?
Aside from local taxes on real estate and some business equipment, California isn’t in the business of valuing and taxing personal property.
Prop. 40 would require the state, within six months, to create a way to assess the value of a wide range of holdings: billionaires’ stock, investment accounts and business interests, but also their art collections, wine vaults, cars and anything else that stores wealth.
“I have a client who has a machine gun collection,” said Jon Feldhammer, a San Francisco tax attorney who said he is advising several clients who would be or believe they could be subject to the billionaire tax.
The definition of wealth and property has to be broad to close possible loopholes, said Kirk Stark, a UCLA tax law professor.
“Otherwise there would be a very simple workaround, which is, if there’s something that’s exempt then you know there would be an incentive to just shift wealth from one form to another,” Stark said.
Ensuring those subject to the tax aren’t underreporting their assets would require the state’s Franchise Tax Board to hire more people for appraisals and auditing, Stark said.
“It can be done,” he said. “But it’s going to take a huge investment of resources to actually pull it off.”
Franchise Tax Board spokesperson Andrew LePage declined to say how many staff the agency would need to implement Prop. 40. Currently, the board doesn’t appraise property but sometimes auditors “examine asset values reported by taxpayers to ensure accuracy,” he said.
Chris Parker, a former attorney for the tax board who now works as a tax attorney with the firm Baker Tilly, said the board has “no way of knowing anyone’s net wealth.”

Ariel Jurow Kleiman, a tax policy professor at the University of Southern California, doesn’t think the state would have a hard time putting the tax into effect. Stocks, which make up a substantial part of billionaires’ wealth, are easily valued, she said. For more “bespoke” property like art and jewelry, California could look to the Internal Revenue Service’s federal tax on inherited property.
“There are commonsense methods like looking at comparable assets or looking to available markets to see how comps are valued,” she said. “We wouldn’t be asking people to reinvent the wheel here.”
Experts do expect disputes over the value of privately held businesses.

Feldhammer said many startup founders have raised money for their companies but haven’t yet sold any products. He criticized the ballot measure for defining a company’s worth as the most recent amount of investment money it raised, which diverges from how the IRS calculates an asset’s fair market value for the estate tax.
“How do you value a company that is not on the public market? It doesn’t even have a product yet. It’s not making any money,” he said.
He said he expects clients to mount lengthy legal challenges arguing the law overvalues their business holdings.
“These are people who have oftentimes plenty of wealth to spend on legal fees to put up the best defense money can buy,” he said.
Will billionaires leave?
The campaign against the measure warns that billionaires will flee California (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/06/california-unions-billionaire-tax-ballot/), depriving the state of billions of dollars in income tax revenue that helps fund the state budget. Experts say there’s no way to know whether the tax will spark a large-scale exodus.
Joel Slemrod, a University of Michigan economics professor who studies tax policy, said there’s very little evidence to gauge how billionaires could react to California’s tax, partly because the proposal is unique.
California experts considering the tax have looked at wealth taxes in European countries to try to discern the impact of Prop. 40. In 1990, 12 countries had wealth taxes. Today, only four remain. Many countries abandoned them because they were difficult and expensive to implement, according to the Organisation for Economic Co-Operation and Development (https://www.oecd.org/en/publications/the-role-and-design-of-net-wealth-taxes-in-the-oecd_9789264290303-en.html). But Slemrod said those examples are “not immediately applicable” to Prop. 40 because they differed significantly in design: Tax rates were much lower, they were intended to be permanent and the money was not earmarked for special interests.
“I wouldn’t jump from the evidence we have to California,” Slemrod said.
But one issue that could matter significantly for California, Slemrod said, is that it is much easier to move assets between states than between countries, as sometimes happened in Europe. Spain allowed its provinces to enact wealth taxes and research suggests that rich people changed residences based on tax rates. (https://direct.mit.edu/rest/article-abstract/101/2/214/58521/Relocation-of-the-Rich-Migration-in-Response-to)
Researchers at the Hoover Institution (https://www.hoover.org/research/net-present-value-billionaire-tax-act-assessment-fiscal-effects-californias-proposed), a conservative policy think tank, conducted an analysis suggesting Californians need not look at history to figure out Prop. 40’s impact. Tax flight has already happened. They estimate that billionaires representing 30% of the tax base have publicly said they have left, lowering state revenue estimates by $60 billion and permanently altering California’s income tax collection.
Feldhammer, the tax lawyer, said “a third to half” of his clients have left the state over the proposed tax. He declined to say how many clients that is. Other tax lawyers told CalMatters that clients who are worth less than $1 billion are also considering moving to avoid limiting their earning potential.
Billionaires who didn’t leave before Jan. 1 would face taxes on their assets anyway; the measure would apply to anyone who was a California resident on that date.
But Feldhammer said he expects people to sue over the measure’s retroactive nature, pointing to two U.S. Supreme Court decisions from the 1920s that held it was unconstitutional to apply the federal estate and gift taxes to assets transferred before those laws were enacted. In 1994, the court ruled that retroactive taxes could be constitutional in certain limited circumstances.
Asked how he’s advising clients who are considering leaving California, Feldhammer said there’s a “reasonable argument that the law may be unconstitutionally retroactive — but to take advantage of that, you’re going to have to leave.”
Would it allow the state to tax my retirement?
If you’re not a billionaire, no.
Even for billionaires, Prop. 40 exempts pensions and individual retirement accounts from the asset tax. There are some exceptions, most notably for Roth IRAs that contain more than $10 million.
Misleading advertisements from opponents claim the tax would allow California soon to eat into retirement savings for average Californians. They’re supporting Prop. 42, which would block the proposed billionaire tax by broadly banning any new taxes on personal property such as investment, retirement and pension accounts. Brin’s political spending group, Building a Better California, put it on the ballot, and unions representing firefighters, police and construction workers support it. (If both measures pass, (https://calmatters.org/health/2026/09/california-wealth-tax-prop-40-41-42/) whichever receives more “yes” votes becomes law.)
Proponents of Prop. 42 say their measure would protect the pensions and retirement accounts of teachers, firefighters and middle-class workers from being taxed before they withdraw the money.
“A new tax on Californians’ retirement and life savings would be devastating,” Robert Gutierrez, president of the California Taxpayers Association, said in a press release.
There are no active proposals to tax those accounts on the ballot or in the Legislature. Lawmakers who have floated such wealth taxes in the past have gotten nowhere.
Still, Brian Marvel, president of the Peace Officers Research Association of California, which supports Prop. 42, denied being deceptive and said it’s “within the realm of realization” for California to tax middle-class workers’ retirement accounts.
“I think it’s more important to be proactive in this area,” he said.
How would the money be used?
Proponents say the billionaire tax is intended to backfill federal cuts to the state’s expansive Medi-Cal health program (https://calmatters.org/health/2026/08/medi-cal-the-cut-healthcare-threatened/) for low-income residents. State officials project the cuts, enacted as part of President Donald Trump’s 2025 budget bill known as H.R. 1, could amount to $30 billion a year (https://calmatters.org/health/2026/08/the-cut-medi-cal-ripple-effects/).
The initiative gives the Legislature broad authority to decide how to spend the money. Of the revenue, 90% percent would be put in a special fund for healthcare; the other 10% would be put in a special fund to pay for schools and food assistance like CalFresh, which was also targeted by federal cuts.
If the money is used to keep Californians on Medi-Cal, that could mean spending it on the private health insurance companies that the state contracts with to administer low-income residents’ coverage.
There is some debate over whether the money would actually offset the cuts to Medi-Cal and how strictly the language bars lawmakers from using the money for anything else.
Opponents such as the California Medical Association and Planned Parenthood recently circulated a memo (https://calmatters.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Memo_Health-Care-Funding-Under-Prop-40_9.18.26.pdf) arguing there’s no guarantee the money would replace the federal funding cuts, because the proposition also allows the money to offset state cuts to Medi-Cal. They warn that would allow lawmakers and the governor to use the new tax money to maintain state funding levels for Medi-Cal and free up the state’s general fund to pay for other things.
Lawmakers and governors have in the past used special new funds to simply replace existing funding. Then-Gov. Arnold Schwarzenegger, a Republican, did it with mental health funding created by a voter-approved tax on millionaires, and then-Gov. Jerry Brown, a Democrat, did it with health funding created by the state tobacco tax. More recently, doctors and hospitals accused Newsom of using a different healthcare tax to backfill the general fund. They placed Proposition 35 on the ballot in 2024 (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2024/11/election-result-proposition-35/) to earmark the money. Voters approved it, but the groups say some funding was still diverted.
But proponents of Prop. 40 said that concern doesn’t make sense: Those budget maneuvers, they said, are usually done to address state budget shortfalls, while Prop. 40 was already written to create funding for a shortfall.
For the record: This story has been updated to correct the amount that Brin has donated to a political action committee opposing Prop. 40 and supporting Props. 41 and 42. He has donated $102 million.

Issue Brief
What Would Proposition 42 Mean for California?
Understanding the Prohibition on Taxing Certain Assets and Enacting Retroactive Taxes
September 2026 | By Kayla Kitson (https://calbudgetcenter.org/people/kayla-kitson/)
Print Issue Brief
key takeaway
Prop. 42 would prohibit new taxes on the ownership of certain assets as well as taxes that apply retroactively. The primary intent of the measure is to invalidate Prop. 40 — the one-time billionaire tax measure also appearing on the November ballot — if it receives more votes, and it would also create new barriers to raising progressive state revenue in the future to adequately meet the needs of Californians.
What Would Prop. 42 Do?
Prop. 42 would amend the state Constitution to prohibit taxes on the ownership of certain assets and on certain retroactive taxes.
Prohibition on New Taxes on Assets
Prop. 42 would prohibit the imposition of any new state tax — enacted on or after January 1, 2026 — on the ownership of financial assets (such as bank accounts, stocks, bonds, or mutual funds), retirement accounts, interests in businesses, intellectual property, and other personal property (such as vehicles, jewelry, artwork, and other movable, physical property).
Prohibition on Retroactive Taxes
Prop. 42 would prohibit the imposition of new retroactive taxes, specifically any tax that is based on “conduct, activities, or a status” that preceded the effective date of the tax. The measure also explicitly prohibits taxes based on someone’s residency status prior to the tax going into effect. An exception would be made for retroactive taxes in cases where the revenues would be used to respond to a governor-declared emergency and the tax does not apply retroactively for more than one year before the effective date.
What Would Prop. 42 Mean for Californians and the State Budget?
The primary intent of Prop. 42 is to invalidate Prop. 40 (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/billionaire-tax-explained-what-proposition-40-would-mean-for-california/), which would create a one-time tax on the wealth of billionaires. The tax would apply retroactively to billionaires who were California residents on January 1, 2026 and would apply to financial assets like stocks and bonds and other types of assets that would put it in direct conflict with Prop. 42’s prohibition of such taxes — though Prop. 40 would exclude retirement accounts, which is a key focus of Prop. 42. If both measures were to pass and Prop. 42 received more votes, Prop. 40 would likely be invalidated.
But the measure would also have more far-reaching consequences by making it harder for state leaders to raise revenues from wealthy households to effectively meet the needs of Californians and to quickly adapt to changing circumstances.
This would come at a time when California is facing challenges on multiple fronts — the consequences of the steep federal cuts to health care and food assistance enacted in H.R. 1 (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/timeline-of-funding-cuts-to-medi-cal-and-calfresh-in-california/), the sustained high poverty rate (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/poverty-in-california-remains-steady-among-the-highest-in-the-nation/), the ongoing housing affordability and homelessness crises, and rising costs of maintaining current services due to inflation and an aging population. Addressing these issues and ensuring California communities can thrive will require the state to substantially raise ongoing revenues (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/building-an-affordable-california-requires-public-investment/).
While Prop. 42 would reduce the options state policymakers have to increase revenues, California voters may still be able to amend the state Constitution in the future to allow a new tax on assets or one that applied retroactively. However, legal challenges are possible and there is no absolute certainty on how courts would rule.
Impacts of Prohibition on Taxing Assets
Currently, the ownership of assets is generally not taxed in California, with the exception of local property taxes on real estate — already subject to strict constitutional limits under Prop. 13 (1978) — and some types of personal property including boats, planes, and business equipment, as well as state vehicle license fees.
While the state does not currently tax (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/billionaire-tax-explained-what-proposition-40-would-mean-for-california/#h-what-is-the-difference-between-income-and-wealth) the ownership of financial assets, business interests, or other intangible assets, it is not constitutionally barred from doing so. Prop. 42 would enshrine this prohibition in the state Constitution, which would prevent state leaders from creating wealth-based taxes in the future. This would limit the options policymakers have to raise progressive revenue to maintain and improve state services that support Californians in staying healthy, housed, and economically secure.
While most Californians hold assets in some form, such as checking or savings accounts, some types of assets are far more likely to be held by wealthy households. For example, about two-thirds of Californians in the top 25% of the wealth distribution hold stocks, bonds, or mutual funds, compared to only 9% of Californians in the bottom 25%, according to an analysis by the Public Policy Institute of California (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/0525ttr-appendix.pdf).
Current federal and state tax policies allow some large wealth increases to never be taxed. California — like the federal government — only taxes the income people receive when they sell their assets, but does not tax the growth in value of assets they hold onto. This growth is known as an unrealized capital gain, and for very wealthy households, unrealized capital gains make up a large share of their total wealth. Some wealthy people may even be able to avoid paying income taxes entirely in some years by not taking a salary, not selling any stocks or other assets, and simply borrowing against their wealth to pay their bills.
Additionally, if someone holds onto assets until their death, their heirs do not have to pay any tax on the gain due to a provision in both federal and state law known as “stepped-up basis,” estimated to cost California around $5 billion each year.
For these reasons, broadly prohibiting state leaders from enacting any new taxes on assets would narrow the options available to ensure that the wealthiest Californians pay their fair share to support the services that benefit residents across the state.
Impacts of Prohibition on Retroactive Taxes
Many federal and state tax law changes have modest retroactivity periods, such as looking back to the beginning of a tax year. This has the benefit of reducing taxpayers’ ability to engage in activities to avoid or evade the tax before it goes into effect, which would reduce the revenue potential. Looking back to the start of the current tax year can also more immediately raise revenues when there are urgent needs.
Broadly prohibiting retroactive taxation would hamstring the ability of state leaders to enact effective and timely tax policy changes that raise revenues needed to meet the needs of Californians.
Who Supports and Opposes Prop. 42?
The top contributor to the Prop. 41 campaign is a group called “Building a Better California,” which is largely funded (https://cal-access.sos.ca.gov/Campaign/Committees/Detail.aspx?id=1486767&view=received) by Google cofounder Sergey Brin and other billionaires. This group is also opposing Prop. 40 and supporting Prop. 41 (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/what-would-proposition-41-mean-for-california/). The measure is also endorsed by the California Republican Party, the California Chamber of Commerce, the California Taxpayers Association, the California Professional Firefighters, and the State Building & Construction Trades Council of California.
There is no official opposition campaign for Prop. 41, but prominent opponents include the Service Employees International Union – United Health Workers West (SEIU-UHW) — the main proponent of the Prop. 40 billionaire tax measure — as well as other labor groups including the California Federation of Teachers and the California Federation of Labor Unions. The California Democratic Party and the League of Women Voters are also opposed.
